optionAnalysis.reason: Not empty: $q_2 \xrightarrow{\epsilon} q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1$ already survives the first symbol.
$q_3$ is lost on the final $a$ ($\delta(q_3, a) = \emptyset$), and $q_2$ is in the closure of $q_1$.
That is the set after $ab$, before reading the last $a$.

pitfalls: Forgetting to take the ε-closure of the start state $q_2$ (which reaches $q_0$).
cse-2017-2-cs-39.verification: Witness paths: $q_2 \xrightarrow{\epsilon} q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{\epsilon} q_2 \xrightarrow{\epsilon} q_0 \xrightarrow{b} q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1$, then $\epsilon$-moves reach $q_2$ and $q_0$; no path ends in $q_3$ after the last $a$.

cse-2017-2-cs-40.approach: Classify each language: unary non-regular languages are not CFLs; $L_2$ needs only one counter; $L_3$ needs two comparisons; $L_4$ is the classic DCFL.

steps.title: L1 and L2
steps.body: $L_1$: every CFL over a one-letter alphabet is regular (Parikh), and $\{a^p : p \text{ prime}\}$ is not regular, so $L_1$ is not CFL → **I false**. $L_2$: push $b$'s, pop one per two $c$'s; $a^n$ is free → CFL → **II false**.

steps.title: L3 and L4
steps.body: $L_3 = \{a^n b^n c^{2n}\}$ needs two equalities → not CFL (pumping), but a TM decides it → **III true**. $L_4 = \{a^n b^n : n \ge 1\}$ is accepted by a DPDA → **IV true**.

steps.title: Select
steps.body: Correct statements: III and IV only → (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: I and II are both false.
II is false ($L_2$ is context-free).
I is false ($L_1$ is not context-free).
III and IV are exactly the true statements — correct.

pitfalls: Believing $\{a^p\}$ is context-free: unary CFLs are always regular.
cse-2017-2-cs-40.verification: Grammar for $L_2$: $S \to aS \mid B$, $B \to bBcc \mid \epsilon$ — confirms II is false.

cse-2017-2-cs-41.approach: Recall the standard decidability table: membership for regular expressions and emptiness for CFGs are decidable; CFG universality ($= \Sigma^*$) and TM membership are undecidable.

steps.title: Decidable ones
steps.body: I: convert $R$ to a DFA and run it on $w$ — decidable. II: mark generating variables and check whether $S$ is generating — decidable.

steps.title: Undecidable ones
steps.body: III: universality of CFGs is undecidable (reduction from PCP / TM computation histories). IV: $A_{TM}$ is undecidable. Answer: III and IV only.

optionAnalysis.reason: I is decidable.
II is decidable.
II is decidable.
III and IV are the undecidable ones — correct.

pitfalls: Confusing CFG emptiness (decidable) with CFG universality (undecidable).

cse-2017-2-cs-42.approach: For a T flip-flop, $T = Q \oplus Q^+$. Compute $T_1, T_0$ for each row and minimise.

steps.title: Minimise
steps.body: $T_1 = 1$ only for $01$: $T_1 = \bar Q_1 Q_0$. $T_0 = 0$ only for $11$: $T_0 = \overline{Q_1 Q_0} = \bar Q_1 + \bar Q_0$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $T_1 = Q_1Q_0$ toggles $Q_1$ in state 11 (11 → 01), breaking saturation.
Matches both excitation columns — correct.
$T_1 = Q_1 + Q_0$ toggles $Q_1$ in state 10, sending it to 01.
$T_0 = Q_1 + Q_0$ is 0 in state 00, so 00 would stay at 00.

pitfalls: Writing $T = Q^+$ (that is the D flip-flop rule).

cse-2017-2-cs-43.approach: Both inner loops swap when the left element is smaller, so this is a cocktail-shaker sort into **descending** order. Trace until a pass makes no swap and read index 3.

scene.caption: Pass 1, forward loop: 1 sinks to the end
Pass 1, backward loop: 6 rises to the front

steps.title: Pass 2
steps.body: Forward: only $i = 2$ ($3 < 4$) swaps → $6,5,4,3,2,1$. Backward: no swaps. done $= 0$ (a swap happened).

steps.title: Pass 3 and output
steps.body: No swaps, done stays 1, loop exits. $\texttt{array} = \{6,5,4,3,2,1\}$, so $\texttt{array[3]} = 3$.

pitfalls: Assuming ascending order and answering 4.
cse-2017-2-cs-43.verification: Any correct sort of {3,5,1,4,6,2} into descending order gives 6,5,4,3,2,1, whose index-3 element is 3.

cse-2017-2-cs-44.approach: Only $Y$ is shared, so the precedence graph has one edge whose direction is decided by the $Y$ operations. Count interleavings where all of one transaction's $Y$-ops precede the other's.

steps.title: When is it serializable?
steps.body: Conflicts are only among $r_1(Y), w_1(Y)$ and $r_2(Y), w_2(Y)$. Serializable as $T_1 \to T_2$ iff $w_1(Y)$ precedes $r_2(Y)$; as $T_2 \to T_1$ iff $w_2(Y)$ precedes $r_1(Y)$. Any other interleaving creates a cycle.

steps.title: Order T1 → T2
steps.body: $w_1(Y)$ is $T_1$'s last op and $r_2(Y)$ is $T_2$'s first, so $T_1$ must run entirely first: $1$ schedule.

steps.title: Order T2 → T1
steps.body:
Need $r_2(Y), w_2(Y)$ before $r_1(Y)$. Let $k \ge 2$ be the number of $T_2$ ops before $r_1(Y)$. Before it: $r_1(X), w_1(X)$ and $k$ ops of $T_2$ → $\binom{k+2}{2}$ ways; after it: $w_1(Y)$ and $4 - k$ ops of $T_2$ → $5 - k$ ways.

$k = 2$: $6 \times 3 = 18$; $k = 3$: $10 \times 2 = 20$; $k = 4$: $15 \times 1 = 15$. Total $= 18 + 20 + 15 = 53$.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $53 + 1 = 54$ conflict-serializable schedules (out of $\binom84 = 70$).

pitfalls: Forgetting the serial schedule $T_1 T_2$.
Counting only the two serial schedules.
cse-2017-2-cs-44.verification: Complement: non-serializable schedules have $r_1(Y)$ before $w_2(Y)$ and $r_2(Y)$ before $w_1(Y)$; $70 - 54 = 16$ of them.

cse-2017-2-cs-45.approach: Compute the average read time separately for instruction fetches (I-cache → L2 → memory) and operand fetches (D-cache → L2 → memory) using the hierarchical formula $T = t_1 + (1-h_1)(t_2 + (1-h_2)t_m)$, then weight them 60 : 40.
cse-2017-2-cs-45.given:
| Level | Access time | Hit ratio |
|---|---|---|
| I-cache | 2 ns | 0.8 |
| D-cache | 2 ns | 0.9 |
| L2 | 8 ns | 0.9 |
| Memory | 90 ns | 1 |

steps.title: Time seen on an L1 miss
steps.body:
An L1 miss always goes to L2 (8 ns), and an L2 miss also goes to memory (90 ns):
$$t_{L2\text{ path}} = 8 + (1-0.9)\times 90 = 8 + 9 = 17\text{ ns}$$
Dirty bit 0 means no write-back cost; referred-word-first means the word is delivered as soon as it arrives, so access times simply add.

cse-2017-2-cs-45.shortcut: Compute the common L2 miss-path time (17 ns) once, then reuse it for both L1 caches.
pitfalls: Using one L1 hit ratio for all reads — the I- and D-caches have different hit ratios.
Forgetting the L2 time on an L2 miss (hierarchical access adds 2 + 8 + 90).

cse-2017-2-cs-46.approach: Evaluate each subquery first. No Spain rows exist, so `> ALL (empty set)` is true for every row; `> ANY` over Germany's goals means "greater than the minimum German score". Count the rows above that minimum.

steps.title: > ALL over Spain
steps.body: No player has country = 'Spain', so the subquery returns the empty set. `x > ALL (∅)` is vacuously **true**, so this condition filters nothing.

steps.title: > ANY over Germany
steps.body: German goals: $\{16, 14, 11, 10, 10\}$. `goals > ANY(...)` holds when goals exceed at least one of them, i.e. $\text{goals} > \min = 10$.

steps.title: Count rows with goals > 10
steps.body: Klose 16, Ronaldo 15, G Müller 14, Fontaine 13, Pelé 12, Klinsmann 11, Kocsis 11 → **7** rows. All six players with 10 goals are excluded.

cse-2017-2-cs-46.shortcut: `> ANY` ≡ `> MIN`, `> ALL` ≡ `> MAX` (and `> ALL` of an empty set is always true).
pitfalls: Treating `> ALL (empty)` as false (that would give 0).
Using `>=` and counting the 10-goal players.
cse-2017-2-cs-46.verification: 13 rows total, 6 of them have exactly 10 goals; 13 − 6 = 7.

cse-2017-2-cs-47.approach: Expand $\frac{1}{(1-z)^3} = \sum \binom{n+2}{2} z^n$; multiplying by $(1+z)$ adds a shifted copy, giving a closed form for $a_n$.

steps.title: Coefficients of the two parts
steps.body: $$\frac{1}{(1-z)^3} = \sum_{n\ge 0} \binom{n+2}{2} z^n,\qquad \frac{z}{(1-z)^3} = \sum_{n\ge 1} \binom{n+1}{2} z^n$$

pitfalls: Using $\binom{n+3}{3}$ (that is for $(1-z)^{-4}$).

cse-2017-2-cs-48.approach: Expand the square and use linearity of expectation with the Poisson facts $E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda = 5$.

steps.title: Second moment
steps.body: $E[X^2] = \operatorname{Var}(X) + (E[X])^2 = 5 + 5^2 = 30$.

pitfalls: Computing $(E[X]+2)^2 = 49$ — that ignores the variance.

cse-2017-2-cs-49.approach: The order $p$ of a B+ tree is the maximum number of child pointers in an internal node: $p$ pointers and $p-1$ keys must fit in one block.

steps.title: Capacity inequality
steps.body: $$p\cdot 2 + (p-1)\cdot 8 \le 512$$

steps.title: Solve
steps.body: $$10p - 8 \le 512 \;\Rightarrow\; 10p \le 520 \;\Rightarrow\; p \le 52$$ So the maximum order is $p = 52$.

pitfalls: Dividing 512 by (8 + 2) = 51.2 → 51, which forgets that an internal node has one more pointer than keys.

cse-2017-2-cs-50.approach: Build the Huffman tree by repeatedly merging the two smallest probabilities, read off each code length (depth), and compute $100 \times \sum p_i \ell_i$.

steps.title: Merge 2
steps.body: Smallest two: S (0.19) and P (0.22) → 0.41. Remaining: 0.25, 0.34, 0.41.

scene.caption: Depths: S, P, Q = 2; T, R = 3

cse-2017-2-cs-50.shortcut: Expected length = sum of all internal-node weights: $0.25 + 0.41 + 0.59 + 1.00 = 2.25$.
pitfalls: Merging S with 0.25 instead of the two smallest (0.19, 0.22).
Answering 2.25 (per character) instead of 225 for 100 characters.
cse-2017-2-cs-50.verification: Internal-node sum $0.25 + 0.41 + 0.59 + 1.00 = 2.25$ matches the depth-weighted sum.

cse-2017-2-cs-51.approach: Simulate preemptive priority scheduling: at every arrival, the ready process with the smallest priority number runs. Then waiting time = completion − arrival − burst.

steps.title: Up to t = 5
steps.body: P1 (pri 2) runs 0–2. At 2, P4 (pri 1) arrives and preempts (P1 has 9 left). At 5, P2 (pri 0) arrives and preempts P4 (P4 has 7 left).

steps.title: P2 runs to completion
steps.body: P2 has the highest priority, so it runs 5–33 even though P5 (t = 9) and P3 (t = 12) arrive meanwhile.

cse-2017-2-cs-51.shortcut: Total waiting = sum of completion times − sum of arrivals − sum of bursts = $240 - 28 - 67 = 145$; $145/5 = 29$.
pitfalls: Treating a larger number as higher priority (here 0 is highest).
Running it non-preemptively.
cse-2017-2-cs-51.verification: CPU is never idle (all bursts sum to 67 and the last process finishes at 67). Shortcut sum $49+33+51+40+67 = 240$; $240 - 28 - 67 = 145$.

cse-2017-2-cs-52.approach: Since 2 is a root, substitute $\lambda = 2$ to find $a$, then factor the cubic and read off the eigenvalues.

steps.title: Factor
steps.body: $$\lambda^3 - 4\lambda^2 - 11\lambda + 30 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 15) = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5)(\lambda + 3)$$ Eigenvalues: $2, 5, -3$.

pitfalls: Answering 3 by confusing the largest |λ| with the absolute value of the negative root.

cse-2017-2-cs-53.approach: Split the 32-bit physical address into tag | line index | block offset for a direct-mapped cache.

steps.title: Offset and index
steps.body: Block size $32 = 2^5$ → offset = 5 bits. Lines $512 = 2^9$ → index = 9 bits.

steps.title: Tag
steps.body: $$\text{tag} = 32 - 9 - 5 = 18\text{ bits}$$

pitfalls: Using cache size instead of line count for the index.
cse-2017-2-cs-53.verification: Equivalently, memory has $2^{32}/2^5 = 2^{27}$ blocks sharing $2^9$ lines: $2^{27}/2^9 = 2^{18}$ blocks per line → 18 tag bits.

cse-2017-2-cs-54.approach: Trace the variables line by line, remembering that `++m` increments before use while `m++` uses the old value first.

steps.title: n = ++m
steps.body: `m` becomes 11, then `n = 11`.

steps.title: n1 = m++
steps.body: `n1` gets the old value 11, then `m` becomes 12.

steps.title: n -= n1
steps.body: $n = 10 - 10 = 0$; the program prints **0**.

pitfalls: Giving n1 the value 12 (post-increment yields the old value).
cse-2017-2-cs-54.verification: n and n1 both start at 11 and are each decremented once, so their difference is 0.

cse-2017-2-cs-55.approach: `i[p]` is the same as `p[i]`. Turn the two characters into ASCII codes, simplify the pointer offset, and take strlen of the remaining suffix.

steps.title: Pointer offset
steps.body: $$c + 84 - 73 - 1 = c + 10$$ which points at "17".

steps.title: strlen
steps.body: `strlen("17") = 2`, so the output is **2**.

pitfalls: Indexing from 1 (taking A and C).
Thinking `2[p]` is invalid syntax.
cse-2017-2-cs-55.verification: Only the difference matters: 'T' − 'I' = 11 letters apart, so the offset is $11 - 1 = 10$, leaving 12 − 10 = 2 characters.
